consumption.simple: The using up of food, energy, money, or other resources.
consumption.detailed: The amount of a resource that people, machines, or systems use, especially when writers discuss waste, demand, or sustainability.
consumption.example: The poster asked families to cut electricity consumption during the heatwave.
consumption.basic: The poster asked families to use less electricity.

contamination.simple: The spoiling of something clean by mixing in dirt, chemicals, or germs.
contamination.detailed: Unwanted matter that enters water, food, soil, or a sample and makes the results unsafe or unreliable.
contamination.example: The creek test showed contamination after the storm washed rubbish downstream.
contamination.basic: The creek was dirty after the storm.

continuity.simple: The way something keeps going without a sudden break.
continuity.detailed: An unbroken link across time or steps, so a story, tradition, or process still feels connected even when details change.
continuity.example: The museum display showed continuity between older tools and the ones farmers still use.
continuity.basic: The museum showed that old and new tools are linked.

contradiction.simple: A clash between two ideas that cannot both be true at once.
contradiction.detailed: A statement, fact, or action that goes against another, so a reader must notice the conflict and decide what to trust.
contradiction.example: There was a contradiction between the witness notes and the photograph of the same street.
contradiction.basic: The notes and the photo did not match.

controversy.simple: A public disagreement that people feel strongly about.
controversy.detailed: A disputed issue that divides a community because the facts, values, or consequences are contested in the media or in civic debate.
controversy.example: The new freeway plan caused controversy because some suburbs would lose parkland.
controversy.basic: People argued about the new freeway plan.

convention.simple: An accepted custom, or a large formal meeting of people who share a purpose.
convention.detailed: A usual rule of behaviour that a group treats as normal, or an organised gathering where delegates discuss a shared issue.
convention.example: In the Federation inquiry, students asked which voting convention women could not yet follow.
convention.basic: Students asked about the old voting custom.

conviction.simple: A strong, settled belief that something is true or right.
conviction.detailed: A firmly held view, often used in argument writing when a speaker stands by a claim with confidence rather than guessing.
conviction.example: She argued with conviction that the school should ban single-use plastic at the canteen.
conviction.basic: She really believed the school should ban the plastic.

cooperation.simple: Working together to reach a shared goal.
cooperation.detailed: Joint action in which people or groups share tasks, information, or resources instead of competing or acting alone.
cooperation.example: The bushfire recovery plan depended on cooperation between councils and local volunteers.
cooperation.basic: Councils and volunteers had to work together.

coordination.simple: The skilful organising of people or parts so they work in time with one another.
coordination.detailed: The planned linking of actions, groups, or body movements so effort is not wasted and the result is orderly.
coordination.example: Rescue work improved once there was better coordination between the police and the SES.
coordination.basic: Rescue work improved when the groups organised themselves.

correlation.simple: A link that shows two things change together, without proving one causes the other.
correlation.detailed: A statistical or observed relationship between variables; science writing must not treat the link as a cause unless further tests support it.
correlation.example: There was a correlation between rainfall and mosquito numbers, but the class still tested other causes.
correlation.basic: Rain and mosquitoes seemed linked, but the class kept checking.

counterpart.simple: A person or thing that has the same role as another in a different place or group.
counterpart.detailed: A matching figure, office, or object that performs a parallel function, often used when comparing countries, teams, or texts.
counterpart.example: The Year 6 mayor wrote to her counterpart in the sister school in Aotearoa New Zealand.
counterpart.basic: The Year 6 mayor wrote to the student who had the same job at the other school.

credibility.simple: The quality of being believable and worth trusting.
credibility.detailed: How far a source, witness, or argument deserves confidence, based on evidence, expertise, and a fair method.
credibility.example: The blog lost credibility when readers found the photographs had been cropped to hide the rubbish.
credibility.basic: People stopped trusting the blog after the photos were cropped.

crisis.simple: A serious turning point when danger is high and a decision cannot wait.
crisis.detailed: A period of intense difficulty—political, environmental, or personal—when ordinary routines fail and rapid, careful action is needed.
crisis.example: During the water crisis, the town limited garden sprinklers to two mornings a week.
crisis.basic: When water was very short, the town limited garden sprinklers.

critique.simple: A careful judgement of a text or idea that explains strengths and weaknesses.
critique.detailed: A reasoned review, not a rude attack, that tests how well a piece of writing, art, or argument works.
critique.example: Her critique of the camp narrative praised the imagery but asked for a clearer ending.
critique.basic: Her review of the camp story said the ending was unclear.

currency.simple: The money a country uses, or the state of being widely accepted right now.
currency.detailed: Coins and notes in official circulation, and, in academic writing, the quality of an idea still being current and in use.
currency.example: The HASS booklet compared Australian currency before and after decimal changeover in 1966.
currency.basic: The booklet compared Australian money before and after 1966.

curriculum.simple: The planned set of subjects and skills a school is meant to teach.
curriculum.detailed: The organised course of study, including topics, texts, and outcomes, that guides lessons across a year or stage.
curriculum.example: The new curriculum asked Year 6 to write a persuasive text about a local environmental issue.
curriculum.basic: The new school plan asked Year 6 to write a persuasive text.

custody.simple: Legal care and protection of a person, or official keeping of an object or prisoner.
custody.detailed: The duty of looking after a child, artefact, or detainee, including the right to make day-to-day decisions about safety and wellbeing.
custody.example: The court gave both parents shared custody so the children still saw each household.
custody.basic: The court said both parents would look after the children.

database.simple: An organised collection of information that a computer can search quickly.
database.detailed: A structured store of records—names, measurements, or sources—designed so users can retrieve, sort, and update facts accurately.
database.example: The class built a database of bird sightings with date, species, and weather notes.
database.basic: The class made an organised list of bird sightings on the computer.

deadline.simple: The latest time by which a task must be finished.
deadline.detailed: A fixed cut-off that organises school, news, or civic work; missing it can weaken a submission or a whole project.
deadline.example: Oliver set a Sunday night deadline so the scholarship essay could still be proofread.
deadline.basic: Oliver chose a last day so he could still check the essay.

deduction.simple: A conclusion reached by using clues and logical steps.
deduction.detailed: Reasoning that moves from evidence or a general rule to a particular conclusion, as in an investigation or a proof.
deduction.example: From the muddy prints, her deduction was that the fox had crossed the oval after rain.
deduction.basic: From the prints, she worked out that a fox had crossed the oval.

deficit.simple: The amount by which something, especially money, falls short of what is needed.
deficit.detailed: A shortfall when spending, rainfall, or another measure is less than income, supply, or a required level.
deficit.example: The council report showed a deficit after the pool repairs cost more than planned.
deficit.basic: The council had spent more than it had.

delegate.simple: A person chosen to speak or vote on behalf of a larger group.
delegate.detailed: A representative sent to a meeting, parliament, or conference with authority to present the group's views.
delegate.example: Each house elected a delegate to take the waste-sorting plan to the student council.
delegate.basic: Each house chose one person to take the plan to the student council.

demographic.simple: A group of people who share a population feature such as age or location.
demographic.detailed: A slice of a population defined by statistics—age, income, language, or region—used in HASS and media to explain patterns.
demographic.example: The library survey showed one demographic—new migrant families—needed more bilingual picture books.
demographic.basic: The survey showed one group of families needed more bilingual books.

denotation.simple: The plain, dictionary meaning of a word, without extra feeling.
denotation.detailed: The literal sense a word points to, contrasted with connotation, which carries mood, attitude, or cultural flavour.
denotation.example: The denotation of 'home' is a place you live, but the story used it to suggest safety.
denotation.basic: The plain meaning of 'home' is a place you live.

deployment.simple: The sending of people or equipment into position for a task.
deployment.detailed: The organised placement of staff, troops, or resources so they can act where they are most needed.
deployment.example: The SES announced the deployment of extra crews before the flood peak reached town.
deployment.basic: The SES said extra crews were being sent before the flood.

depression.simple: A long period when an economy is weak and many people lose work.
depression.detailed: In HASS, a severe downturn such as the 1930s slump, when trade, wages, and confidence fall and hardship spreads.
depression.example: The inquiry compared family life in the 1930s depression with life during later recessions.
depression.basic: The inquiry compared family life when the economy was very weak.

derivative.simple: Something developed from an earlier work, idea, or substance.
derivative.detailed: A later product, word, or text that comes from a source; in school writing it can also mean work that copies another style too closely.
derivative.example: The teacher said the poem felt derivative because it copied another writer's images almost exactly.
derivative.basic: The teacher said the poem copied another writer's images.

destination.simple: The place someone or something is travelling towards.
destination.detailed: The intended end point of a journey, shipment, or plan, often contrasted with the starting point or the route.
destination.example: The expedition's destination was a research hut on the edge of the ice.
destination.basic: The trip was meant to end at a research hut on the ice.

destruction.simple: The act of ruining something so badly that it cannot be used as before.
destruction.detailed: Severe damage that ends the useful life of a building, habitat, or object, often discussed after war, fire, or careless development.
destruction.example: Habitat destruction along the river left fewer nesting sites for the herons.
destruction.basic: When the river habitat was ruined, fewer herons could nest.

detection.simple: The act of noticing or finding something that was hidden or faint.
detection.detailed: The process of discovering a signal, disease, error, or change, often with instruments or a careful method.
detection.example: Early detection of the leak saved thousands of litres of treated water.
detection.basic: Finding the leak early saved a lot of treated water.

deterioration.simple: The process of becoming worse in quality, strength, or condition.
deterioration.detailed: A gradual decline in health, materials, or an environment, which science notes often measure against a baseline.
deterioration.example: The report tracked deterioration of the coral after the water stayed unusually warm.
deterioration.basic: The report showed the coral getting worse after the warm water.

deviation.simple: A movement away from a planned path, rule, or usual value.
deviation.detailed: The amount or kind of difference from a standard, mean, or expected route, used in science and in descriptions of behaviour.
deviation.example: A small deviation in temperature was enough to change how fast the crystals formed.
deviation.basic: A small change from the usual temperature changed the crystals.

diagnosis.simple: An identification of what is wrong, based on signs and tests.
diagnosis.detailed: A reasoned decision about the cause of a problem—medical, mechanical, or academic—after evidence has been examined.
diagnosis.example: The vet's diagnosis was that the koala was dehydrated after the heatwave.
diagnosis.basic: The vet decided the koala needed water after the heatwave.

diagram.simple: A simple drawing that shows how the parts of something fit or work.
diagram.detailed: A labelled visual model—flow chart, cross-section, or cycle—used to make a process or structure easier to explain.
diagram.example: A labelled diagram of the water cycle earned more marks than a paragraph with no picture.
diagram.basic: A labelled picture of the water cycle earned more marks.

dilemma.simple: A hard choice between two options that both have serious downsides.
dilemma.detailed: A problem in which every available action has a cost, so a writer must weigh values, not just pick an easy winner.
dilemma.example: The waste debate created a dilemma: ban the canteen wrap, or keep it and reduce litter another way.
dilemma.basic: The class had a hard choice about the canteen wrap.

dimension.simple: A measurement of size, or one important side of a problem.
dimension.detailed: A length, width, height, or other measurable extent; in academic writing, also an aspect of an issue that must not be ignored.
dimension.example: Height was only one dimension; the box also had to fit through the storeroom door.
dimension.basic: Height was only one measurement the box needed.

diplomacy.simple: The skill of handling disagreements between groups in a calm, respectful way.
diplomacy.detailed: Official or personal negotiation that seeks agreement without force, using careful language and compromise.
diplomacy.example: The captains used diplomacy instead of shouting when the two teams disputed the catch.
diplomacy.basic: The captains talked calmly instead of shouting about the catch.

directive.simple: An official instruction that tells people what they must do.
directive.detailed: A formal order or written guidance from a leader, council, or department that staff or citizens are expected to follow.
directive.example: A health directive required every camp kitchen to keep raw chicken on a separate board.
directive.basic: A health rule said camp kitchens must keep raw chicken separate.

disability.simple: A long-term condition that can make some everyday activities harder.
disability.detailed: A physical, sensory, or cognitive difference that interacts with barriers in the environment; fair communities remove those barriers.
disability.example: The new ramp showed the school was removing barriers for students with disability.
disability.basic: The new ramp made the school easier to enter for some students.

disaster.simple: A sudden event that causes great damage, loss, or suffering.
disaster.detailed: A natural or human-made catastrophe—flood, fire, quake, or serious accident—that overwhelms ordinary local resources.
disaster.example: After the flood disaster, families slept in the sports hall until the houses dried.
disaster.basic: After the bad flood, families slept in the sports hall.

discipline.simple: A field of study, or the self-control that keeps work steady and fair.
discipline.detailed: A branch of knowledge such as history or biology, and also the trained habit of following methods, rules, or practice routines.
discipline.example: History is a discipline that trains you to test sources instead of copying the first website.
discipline.basic: History is a subject that trains you to test sources.

discourse.simple: Connected talk or writing about a topic, especially in a formal way.
discourse.detailed: The language a community uses to discuss an idea, including the shared terms, tone, and assumptions in a debate or text.
discourse.example: The novel's discourse about belonging mixed First Nations place names with the new settlers' maps.
discourse.basic: The novel's talk about belonging mixed old place names with new maps.

discrepancy.simple: A difference between two records that should have matched.
discrepancy.detailed: An unexplained gap between figures, witness accounts, or measurements that a careful reader must notice and resolve.
discrepancy.example: There was a discrepancy between the rainfall gauge and the Bureau's published total.
discrepancy.basic: The rainfall gauge and the published total did not match.

discretion.simple: The freedom to decide, used carefully and privately.
discretion.detailed: Judgement left to a responsible person when rules do not fix every detail, plus the tact of not sharing what should stay confidential.
discretion.example: Late homework was accepted at the teacher's discretion if a student had been ill.
discretion.basic: The teacher could decide to accept late homework if a student had been ill.

discrimination.simple: Unfair treatment of people because of who they are, or the skill of noticing fine differences.
discrimination.detailed: Unjust action against a group based on race, sex, disability, or similar grounds; in academic use it can also mean careful distinction between ideas.
discrimination.example: The HASS unit examined how discrimination limited who could vote in early Australian elections.
discrimination.basic: The unit examined how unfair rules limited who could vote.

disposition.simple: A person's usual mood or way of treating others.
disposition.detailed: A fairly stable tendency of character—calm, fiery, generous—that shapes how a figure behaves across a narrative.
disposition.example: The narrator's gentle disposition made the harsh boarding-house scenes feel even colder.
disposition.basic: The narrator's gentle nature made the boarding house feel even colder.

dispute.simple: A serious disagreement, often about facts, rights, or a decision.
dispute.detailed: A conflict that may stay verbal or become formal, as when communities, teams, or nations contest a claim.
dispute.example: The two councils entered a dispute over who should pay for the shared bike path.
dispute.basic: The two councils argued over who should pay for the bike path.

disruption.simple: A break that stops something from running in its usual way.
disruption.detailed: An interruption to a system, lesson, or habitat, sometimes useful in experiments but often costly in civic life.
disruption.example: Storm damage caused disruption to the train line, so the excursion left an hour late.
disruption.basic: Storm damage stopped the trains, so the excursion left late.

dissertation.simple: A long, formal piece of writing that investigates one research question.
dissertation.detailed: An extended academic study, usually for a university award, built from sources, method, and a sustained argument.
dissertation.example: Mum's old dissertation on local wetlands still had useful maps for our creek report.
dissertation.basic: Mum's old university paper on wetlands still had useful maps.

distribution.simple: The way things are spread out, or the act of giving them to different people.
distribution.detailed: The pattern of where people, species, or goods are found, and the process of allocating resources across a community.
distribution.example: The map showed an uneven distribution of public libraries across the newer suburbs.
distribution.basic: The map showed that libraries were not spread evenly across the newer suburbs.

diversity.simple: A range of different people, living things, or ideas in one place.
diversity.detailed: Variety within a community or ecosystem, valued in HASS and science because different strengths and species make a system more resilient.
diversity.example: The festival celebrated the cultural diversity of the families in our catchment.
diversity.basic: The festival celebrated how many different family backgrounds were in our area.

doctrine.simple: A set of official beliefs that a group teaches as true.
doctrine.detailed: A formal teaching in religion, law, or politics that members are expected to accept and apply to new cases.
doctrine.example: The class compared one legal doctrine about terra nullius with later High Court decisions.
doctrine.basic: The class compared one official legal teaching with later court decisions.

domain.simple: An area of knowledge, control, or online space that belongs to a person or field.
domain.detailed: A territory of expertise or authority—such as science or a website name—within which certain rules and terms apply.
domain.example: Spelling rules sit in the language domain, but this question also needed science vocabulary.
domain.basic: Spelling rules belong to language, but this question also needed science words.

dominance.simple: The state of having the strongest influence or control.
dominance.detailed: A position of power in which one group, species, or idea outweighs others, sometimes fairly earned and sometimes imposed.
dominance.example: The inquiry asked how British dominance shaped land laws after 1788.
dominance.basic: The inquiry asked how British control shaped land laws after 1788.

duration.simple: The length of time something lasts.
duration.detailed: A measured span from start to finish, used in science and planning when timing is part of the result.
duration.example: Students recorded the duration of each bounce until the ball stayed still.
duration.basic: Students recorded how long each bounce lasted.

dynasty.simple: A family that rules a country for several generations.
dynasty.detailed: A line of rulers from the same family, or a long period named after them, used in HASS to organise change over time.
dynasty.example: The timeline placed each Chinese dynasty beside the inventions it was known for.
dynasty.basic: The timeline placed each ruling family beside its inventions.

ecology.simple: The study of how living things interact with one another and their surroundings.
ecology.detailed: A science that examines relationships among organisms, habitats, and non-living factors such as water, soil, and climate.
ecology.example: Our ecology unit traced how removing one predator changed the whole rock-pool web.
ecology.basic: Our living-systems unit traced how removing one predator changed the rock pool.

edition.simple: A particular published version of a book, paper, or programme.
edition.detailed: One printing or release of a text, which may update facts, images, or wording compared with earlier versions.
edition.example: The revised edition of the atlas corrected the spelling of several First Nations place names.
edition.basic: The newer version of the atlas corrected several place names.

efficiency.simple: Getting a good result without wasting time, energy, or materials.
efficiency.detailed: The ratio of useful output to input; science and design praise methods that achieve the goal with less waste.
efficiency.example: The new tap design improved water efficiency without reducing pressure.
efficiency.basic: The new tap wasted less water without reducing pressure.

elite.simple: A small group with special power, wealth, or skill compared with most people.
elite.detailed: Those at the top of a social, sporting, or academic hierarchy; HASS writing often asks who is included and who is shut out.
elite.example: Only an elite of property-owning men could vote in some early colonial elections.
elite.basic: Only a small top group of property-owning men could vote in some early elections.

enclosure.simple: A fenced or walled space, or something shut inside a letter or package.
enclosure.detailed: Land or an area closed off from common use, and also an extra document included with a letter; HASS may discuss historical fencing-off of shared land.
enclosure.example: The zoo's new enclosure gave the wombats deeper burrows and more shade.
enclosure.basic: The zoo's new fenced space gave the wombats more shade.

encounter.simple: A meeting, especially one that is unexpected or important.
encounter.detailed: A face-to-face or narrative meeting with a person, creature, or idea that can change the course of a story.
encounter.example: The camp narrative hinged on one encounter between the lost hikers and a park ranger.
encounter.basic: The camp story hinged on one meeting between the hikers and a ranger.

endurance.simple: The ability to keep going through pain, effort, or difficulty.
endurance.detailed: Staying power of body or spirit over a long trial, often used in literary portraits of characters who refuse to quit.
endurance.example: The survivor's endurance in the desert chapters made the rescue scene feel earned.
endurance.basic: The survivor's staying power in the desert made the rescue feel earned.

enforcement.simple: The act of making sure a rule or law is actually followed.
enforcement.detailed: Official action—fines, inspections, or court steps—that turns a written rule into practice in a community.
enforcement.example: Without enforcement, the no-fishing zone on the reef was only a sign on a post.
enforcement.basic: Without anyone checking, the no-fishing zone was only a sign.

engagement.simple: Active involvement in a task, community, or idea.
engagement.detailed: The quality of taking part with attention and responsibility, not merely being present; HASS also uses it for civic participation.
engagement.example: Civic engagement rose after the council let students speak at the planning meeting.
engagement.basic: More people took part after the council let students speak.

engine.simple: A machine that turns energy into movement or useful work.
engine.detailed: A device—petrol, electric, or steam—that converts stored energy into motion, heat, or power for transport or industry.
engine.example: The steam engine in the museum still turned the wheel when the guide released the valve.
engine.basic: The old steam machine in the museum still turned the wheel.

enquiry.simple: A careful search for answers by asking questions and checking evidence.
enquiry.detailed: A structured investigation—classroom or official—that gathers sources, tests ideas, and reports findings (Australian spelling of the academic sense).
enquiry.example: The Federation enquiry asked who was left out of the first Commonwealth Parliament.
enquiry.basic: The Federation investigation asked who was left out of the first Parliament.

enterprise.simple: A bold project or a business that takes a risk to achieve something.
enterprise.detailed: An organised venture, commercial or civic, that needs initiative, planning, and often money; also the quality of being enterprising.
enterprise.example: The class enterprise sold seedlings and used the profit for creek-care gloves.
enterprise.basic: The class business sold seedlings and used the profit for gloves.

entity.simple: A thing that exists as a separate unit and can be named.
entity.detailed: A distinct being, organisation, or object treated as one whole in law, science, or academic analysis.
entity.example: The wildlife trust is a legal entity, so it can own the reserve in its own name.
entity.basic: The wildlife trust is a separate organisation, so it can own the reserve.

episode.simple: One event in a series, or one instalment of a story.
episode.detailed: A bounded incident within a longer narrative, history, or television sequence, often with its own turning point.
episode.example: The storm episode in chapter four changed the friendship more than any later scene.
episode.basic: The storm scene in chapter four changed the friendship.

epoch.simple: A long period of time marked by a particular way of life or set of events.
epoch.detailed: A distinctive historical or geological age that historians or scientists use to group major changes.
epoch.example: Federation began a new political epoch, even though everyday life changed slowly.
epoch.basic: Federation began a new political period, even though everyday life changed slowly.

equality.simple: The state of people having the same rights, value, or chances.
equality.detailed: A civic principle that laws and opportunities should not favour one group unfairly over another.
equality.example: The speech claimed that equality before the law still needed fair access to courts.
equality.basic: The speech said equal legal rights still needed fair access to courts.

equilibrium.simple: A steady balance in which opposing forces cancel one another.
equilibrium.detailed: A stable state in a system—physical, chemical, or ecological—until a new factor shifts the balance.
equilibrium.example: The rock pool stayed in equilibrium until extra nutrients made algae take over.
equilibrium.basic: The rock pool stayed balanced until extra nutrients made algae take over.

equity.simple: Fairness that gives people what they need, not only the same thing.
equity.detailed: Justice that notices different starting points, so support is adjusted until chances are genuinely fair.
equity.example: Giving extra reading time was equity, because some students were still learning English.
equity.basic: Giving extra reading time was fair, because some students were still learning English.

equivalent.simple: Something that has the same value, meaning, or effect as something else.
equivalent.detailed: A matching quantity or substitute that can stand in for another measure, word, or role without changing the result.
equivalent.example: Fifty millilitres is the equivalent of about ten teaspoons in the method.
equivalent.basic: Fifty millilitres is about the same as ten teaspoons in the method.

erosion.simple: The wearing away of rock or soil by water, wind, or ice.
erosion.detailed: A physical process that removes material from a landscape or, figuratively, slowly weakens a right, bank, or trust.
erosion.example: Coastal erosion had moved the fence line several metres inland since the last survey.
erosion.basic: The waves had worn the coast so the fence was now further inland.

essay.simple: A short piece of writing that explains or argues one main idea.
essay.detailed: A structured composition with an introduction, developed paragraphs, and a conclusion, used in scholarship and classroom assessment.
essay.example: The scholarship essay had to take a clear position on whether phones belong in class.
essay.basic: The scholarship writing task had to take a clear position on phones in class.

essence.simple: The most important quality that makes something what it is.
essence.detailed: The core nature of an idea or thing, stripped of extra detail, which a precise writer tries to name.
essence.example: In essence, the rule was simple: every claim needed a source the marker could check.
essence.basic: The main point of the rule was simple: every claim needed a source.

ethics.simple: Ideas about what is right and wrong when you make a choice.
ethics.detailed: A system of moral principles used to judge actions, research methods, or public decisions as fair or harmful.
ethics.example: Research ethics meant the class could not stress the minnows just to get a dramatic graph.
ethics.basic: Fair research rules meant the class could not stress the minnows for a dramatic graph.

evolution.simple: Gradual change over a long time, especially in living things.
evolution.detailed: In science, the process by which species change through inherited variation; in general academic use, any slow development of an idea or system.
evolution.example: The display explained evolution with finch beaks that matched different island foods.
evolution.basic: The display explained slow species change with finch beaks that matched island foods.

examination.simple: A formal test, or a close look that checks every important detail.
examination.detailed: A timed assessment of knowledge, and also a careful inspection of evidence, a patient, or a text.
examination.example: Close examination of the diary showed the dates had been added in a different ink.
examination.basic: A close look at the diary showed the dates were in a different ink.

exception.simple: A case that does not follow the usual rule.
exception.detailed: An allowed or observed departure from a pattern, which a precise writer should name so the rule is not overstated.
exception.example: Every group presented on Friday, with the exception of the team whose speaker was ill.
exception.basic: Every group presented on Friday except the team whose speaker was ill.

excerpt.simple: A short passage copied from a longer text.
excerpt.detailed: A selected extract used for close reading, so students can study language or evidence without reprinting the whole work.
excerpt.example: The paper printed an excerpt from the speech, then asked what the metaphor suggested.
excerpt.basic: The paper printed a short piece of the speech, then asked about the metaphor.

excess.simple: More of something than is needed or healthy.
excess.detailed: A surplus beyond a useful or safe amount, whether of nutrients, spending, or emotion, often treated as a problem to reduce.
excess.example: Excess fertiliser washed into the lagoon and fed a thick algal bloom.
excess.basic: Too much fertiliser washed into the lagoon and fed the algae.

exclusion.simple: The act of leaving someone or something out.
exclusion.detailed: A policy or practice that bars people from a place, right, or group, or that omits data from a set for a stated reason.
exclusion.example: The timeline noted the exclusion of many First Nations people from the early electoral rolls.
exclusion.basic: The timeline noted that many First Nations people were left off the early electoral rolls.

excursion.simple: A short trip taken for learning or pleasure.
excursion.detailed: An organised outing from school or camp with a purpose—fieldwork, a museum, or a civic site—and planned safety rules.
excursion.example: The museum excursion let students handle replica artefacts they could not touch on display.
excursion.basic: The museum trip let students handle replica artefacts.

execution.simple: The carrying out of a plan, method, or piece of work.
execution.detailed: How well an intended action is actually performed, from a science method to a speech; in academic tasks the focus is delivery, not punishment.
execution.example: The idea was strong, but poor execution meant the model leaked before the judges arrived.
execution.basic: The idea was strong, but the way they built the model meant it leaked.

exemption.simple: Official permission not to follow a rule that applies to others.
exemption.detailed: A legal or administrative release from a duty, fee, or requirement, granted for a stated reason.
exemption.example: A medical exemption meant she could sit the running test on another day.
exemption.basic: A medical note meant she could sit the running test on another day.

exhibition.simple: A public display of objects, art, or student work.
exhibition.detailed: An organised showing, in a gallery, museum, or hall, designed to teach, persuade, or celebrate what is on view.
exhibition.example: The travelling exhibition of Antarctic photographs filled the library with blue light.
exhibition.basic: The travelling display of Antarctic photographs filled the library with blue light.

exile.simple: The state of being forced to live away from your home country.
exile.detailed: Removal from one's homeland, by law or threat, and the life of a person who cannot safely return.
exile.example: The memoir described childhood in exile after the family fled the civil war.
exile.basic: The memoir described childhood after the family had to leave their country.

existence.simple: The fact of being real or alive.
existence.detailed: The state of having being in the world, or of a problem, species, or idea actually occurring rather than being imagined.
existence.example: Fossils proved the existence of animals that no longer live on this coastline.
existence.basic: Fossils proved that those animals had been real on this coastline.

expansion.simple: The process of becoming larger in size, number, or range.
expansion.detailed: Growth of a city, empire, business, or idea into new space or topics, with costs as well as gains.
expansion.example: Urban expansion had replaced the wetlands with warehouses in less than twenty years.
expansion.basic: The growing city had replaced the wetlands with warehouses.

expectation.simple: A belief about what is likely or required to happen.
expectation.detailed: A forecast or standard that shapes behaviour, from a teacher's academic demand to a community's hope about the future.
expectation.example: The high expectation in the scholarship paper was that every quote would be explained, not dumped.
expectation.basic: The scholarship paper required every quote to be explained, not dumped.

expedition.simple: A journey made for a clear purpose, such as research or exploration.
expedition.detailed: An organised group travel with goals, equipment, and roles, often into difficult country, rather than a casual holiday.
expedition.example: The scientific expedition collected ice cores to compare snowfall across decades.
expedition.basic: The research trip collected ice cores to compare snowfall.

expenditure.simple: The money, time, or energy that is spent.
expenditure.detailed: An amount laid out for a purpose, especially in budgets where writers compare spending with income or need.
expenditure.example: Public expenditure on the new library was defended as an investment in literacy.
expenditure.basic: Public spending on the new library was defended as an investment in literacy.

expense.simple: A cost you have to pay, in money or in something valuable.
expense.detailed: A particular charge or sacrifice; writers also say one gain comes 'at the cost of' another when the second thing is harmed.
expense.example: Faster delivery came at the expense of extra packaging waste.
expense.basic: Faster delivery meant more packaging waste.

expertise.simple: Special skill or knowledge gained through training and practice.
expertise.detailed: Trusted competence in a field that lets someone judge evidence, methods, or craft at a high standard.
expertise.example: The ranger's expertise helped the class tell a goanna track from a large lizard print.
expertise.basic: The ranger's special knowledge helped the class tell the tracks apart.

exposure.simple: The state of being left open to a condition, risk, or public view.
exposure.detailed: Contact with weather, chemicals, ideas, or an audience, which may teach, harm, or reveal something previously hidden.
exposure.example: Long sun exposure without hats was listed as a hazard on the fieldwork sheet.
exposure.basic: Long time in the sun without hats was listed as a hazard.

expression.simple: A word or look that shows a feeling or idea.
expression.detailed: A phrase with a set meaning, or the way emotion and thought are shown in language, art, or the face.
expression.example: The idiom was an old expression, so the footnote explained it for modern readers.
expression.basic: The idiom was an old phrase, so the footnote explained it.

extension.simple: Something added to make a thing longer, larger, or last more time.
extension.detailed: An extra section, deadline, or idea that continues an original piece of work, land, or argument.
extension.example: A one-day extension was granted so the group could finish the bibliography properly.
extension.basic: A one-day extra was granted so the group could finish the bibliography.

extent.simple: How far or how much something reaches.
extent.detailed: The scale, degree, or range of a problem, area, or effect, which precise writing tries to measure rather than call 'huge'.
extent.example: The map showed the extent of the floodplain after two days of rain.
extent.basic: The map showed how far the floodplain reached after two days of rain.

facility.simple: A building or place designed for a particular activity.
facility.detailed: A purpose-built site or service—sports, medical, or research—and, less often, an ease or fluency in doing something.
facility.example: The new sports facility had a rainwater tank that flushed the toilets.
facility.basic: The new sports building had a rainwater tank that flushed the toilets.

faction.simple: A smaller group inside a larger one that pushes its own aims.
faction.detailed: A party within a party, class, or movement whose loyalty to its subgroup can split the whole organisation.
faction.example: One political faction wanted the park sold; another wanted it kept as public land.
faction.basic: One group inside the party wanted the park sold; another wanted it kept.

faculty.simple: The teaching staff of a university, or a natural ability of the mind.
faculty.detailed: A department of academics, and also a power such as memory or reason that a person can train or lose.
faculty.example: A visiting faculty member from the university helped mark the science posters.
faculty.basic: A visiting university teacher helped mark the science posters.

failure.simple: The fact of not succeeding, or of a system stopping as it should.
failure.detailed: An unsuccessful outcome, or a breakdown in a method, machine, or duty, which science writing treats as data rather than shame.
failure.example: The first trial was a useful failure because it showed the battery could not last the night.
failure.basic: The first trial did not work, but it showed the battery could not last the night.

fairness.simple: The quality of treating people and claims in a just, even-handed way.
fairness.detailed: Impartial dealing that weighs evidence and needs without favouring friends, wealth, or a louder voice.
fairness.example: Procedural fairness meant both sides of the waste debate received the same speaking time.
fairness.basic: Being even-handed meant both sides received the same speaking time.

famine.simple: A severe shortage of food that affects many people at once.
famine.detailed: A regional crisis of hunger, often caused by drought, war, or failed harvests, with lasting social effects.
famine.example: The HASS source described a famine that forced whole villages to move toward the coast.
famine.basic: The source described a food crisis that forced whole villages to move.

feedback.simple: Comments that tell you how well something worked and how to improve it.
feedback.detailed: Information returned to a learner, system, or designer—praise, correction, or data—so the next attempt can be better.
feedback.example: Constructive feedback told him which paragraph needed a topic sentence.
feedback.basic: Useful comments told him which paragraph needed a topic sentence.

fieldwork.simple: Learning or research done outside, in the real place being studied.
fieldwork.detailed: First-hand collection of data on site—creek, street, or bush—rather than only from books or a classroom model.
fieldwork.example: Fieldwork at the creek included turbidity tests and a sketch of the banks.
fieldwork.basic: The outdoor research at the creek included water tests and a sketch.

filter.simple: A device or method that lets some things through and blocks others.
filter.detailed: A physical screen, chemical layer, or digital rule that separates wanted from unwanted matter, light, or information.
filter.example: The water filter removed grit, but the class still boiled the sample before tasting nothing.
filter.basic: The strainer removed grit, but the class still boiled the sample.

finance.simple: The management of money for a person, business, or government.
finance.detailed: How funds are raised, spent, and recorded, including budgets, loans, and public accounts in HASS inquiries.
finance.example: The finance committee published how much of the fete profit went to the library.
finance.basic: The money committee published how much of the fete profit went to the library.

flexibility.simple: The ability to bend or change without breaking.
flexibility.detailed: Physical springiness, and also a willingness to adjust a plan, timetable, or method when new evidence appears.
flexibility.example: Timetable flexibility let the class finish the experiment when the rain finally stopped.
flexibility.basic: A changeable timetable let the class finish the experiment after the rain.

fluctuation.simple: An irregular rise and fall in a level or amount.
fluctuation.detailed: Repeated change around a typical value—temperature, prices, or mood—rather than a single steady trend.
fluctuation.example: Temperature fluctuation overnight was enough to crack the drying clay pots.
fluctuation.basic: The changing overnight temperature was enough to crack the clay pots.

formation.simple: The way something is made or arranged, or the process of that happening.
formation.detailed: A shape, group, or rock structure produced by a process, and also the act of coming into being.
formation.example: The sandstone formation along the gorge showed layers from an ancient river.
formation.basic: The sandstone shape along the gorge showed layers from an ancient river.

formula.simple: A rule written in symbols, or a set method that people follow.
formula.detailed: A scientific or mathematical statement of a relationship, and also a trusted recipe for solving a kind of problem.
formula.example: The class used a simple formula to convert the creek depths from centimetres to metres.
formula.basic: The class used a simple rule to convert the creek depths into metres.

forum.simple: A public place or meeting where people exchange views.
forum.detailed: An organised discussion space—hall, online board, or civic assembly—meant for open argument rather than a private chat.
forum.example: The community forum let residents question the landfill plan before the council voted.
forum.basic: The community meeting let residents question the landfill plan.

foundation.simple: The solid base something is built on, or an organisation set up for a purpose.
foundation.detailed: The supporting layer of a building or argument, and also a funded body that supports education, research, or charity.
foundation.example: A solid foundation of evidence made the waste argument harder to dismiss.
foundation.basic: A solid base of evidence made the waste argument harder to dismiss.

fraction.simple: A part of a whole, written as one number over another, or a small share.
fraction.detailed: A rational number showing a division of a unit, and more loosely any portion that is less than the complete amount.
fraction.example: Only a fraction of the surveyed families still used single-use bottles every day.
fraction.basic: Only a small part of the surveyed families still used single-use bottles.

fragment.simple: A small broken piece of something larger.
fragment.detailed: An incomplete scrap of a text, object, or memory that a reader or scientist must interpret without the whole.
fragment.example: A pottery fragment from the dig still showed a painted wave along the rim.
fragment.basic: A small broken piece of pottery still showed a painted wave.

franchise.simple: The right to vote in elections, or a licence to run a business under a larger company's name.
franchise.detailed: In Australian HASS, the civic right to vote; in commerce, a contract that lets a local owner trade with another firm's brand and rules.
franchise.example: The inquiry asked when women in each colony gained the franchise before Federation.
franchise.basic: The inquiry asked when women in each colony gained the right to vote.

frequency.simple: How often something happens in a given time.
frequency.detailed: The count of events per unit of time, or, in physics, the number of wave cycles each second.
frequency.example: The frequency of bus services dropped after six o'clock, which the petition called unfair.
frequency.basic: The buses came less often after six o'clock, which the petition called unfair.

frontier.simple: The far edge of settled land, or of what people yet understand.
frontier.detailed: A borderland between known and unknown country, and figuratively the leading edge of a science or idea.
frontier.example: The novel set its last chapter on a dusty frontier where the maps stopped.
frontier.basic: The novel set its last chapter on a dusty edge of settlement where the maps stopped.

funding.simple: Money provided to pay for a project or organisation.
funding.detailed: Financial support from government, donors, or fees that makes a programme, study, or service possible.
funding.example: Without extra funding, the after-school science club could not replace the broken microscopes.
funding.basic: Without extra money, the science club could not replace the broken microscopes.

gap.simple: A missing space or an important difference between two things.
gap.detailed: A hole in knowledge, provision, or achievement that a writer should name so it can be closed or explained.
gap.example: The marker noted a gap in the evidence between the survey and the final claim.
gap.basic: The marker noted missing evidence between the survey and the final claim.

gauge.simple: An instrument that measures something, or a standard used to judge it.
gauge.detailed: A device or scale for reading a quantity such as rainfall or pressure, and also a way of estimating size or quality.
gauge.example: The rain gauge overflowed, so the weekend total had to be estimated from the Bureau.
gauge.basic: The rain measurer overflowed, so the weekend total had to be estimated.

gender.simple: Being male, female, or another identity, and how societies treat those groups.
gender.detailed: A social and personal category used in HASS to discuss roles, rights, and fairness, distinct from a simple biological label.
gender.example: The unit compared gender roles in 1901 newspaper adverts with roles shown in today's catalogues.
gender.basic: The unit compared men's and women's roles in 1901 adverts with roles shown today.

generation.simple: People born around the same time, or the process of producing something.
generation.detailed: A cohort that shares a historical moment, and also the making of power, ideas, or offspring.
generation.example: Each generation in the oral history remembered the river differently.
generation.basic: Each age group in the oral history remembered the river differently.

geography.simple: The study of Earth's places, landscapes, and how people live in them.
geography.detailed: A HASS field that examines physical features, climate, and human patterns of settlement, work, and movement.
geography.example: Human geography helped explain why the new suburb had so few shady streets.
geography.basic: The study of people and place helped explain why the new suburb had so few shady streets.

gesture.simple: A movement of the body that shows a feeling, or a small symbolic action.
gesture.detailed: A physical sign—wave, shrug, bow—or a limited act meant to express goodwill, protest, or meaning without many words.
gesture.example: A small kind gesture—leaving the last orange—changed how the two rivals spoke after lunch.
gesture.basic: Leaving the last orange changed how the two rivals spoke after lunch.

glacier.simple: A huge, slow-moving mass of ice that shapes the land.
glacier.detailed: A persistent body of ice formed from compacted snow, which carves valleys and stores fresh water over centuries.
glacier.example: The melting glacier had left a new lake that was not on last year's map.
glacier.basic: The melting ice mass had left a new lake that was not on last year's map.

glossary.simple: An alphabetical list that explains special words used in a text.
glossary.detailed: A mini-dictionary at the end of a book or unit, written so readers can check terms without leaving the topic.
glossary.example: The science glossary defined 'turbidity' in one sentence Oliver could actually use.
glossary.basic: The science word list defined 'turbidity' in one sentence he could use.

governance.simple: The way an organisation or country is run and held to account.
governance.detailed: The systems of rules, roles, and oversight that steer public or private bodies, not only the people who happen to lead them.
governance.example: Good governance meant the student council published how it spent the fete money.
governance.basic: Good running of the school groups meant the council published how it spent the money.

gradient.simple: How steep a slope is, or how quickly something changes from one value to another.
gradient.detailed: The rate of change along a line or surface—height, temperature, or concentration—used in science and design.
gradient.example: A steep gradient on the track made the creek water run faster after rain.
gradient.basic: A steep slope on the track made the creek water run faster after rain.

graph.simple: A diagram that shows data as lines, bars, or points.
graph.detailed: A visual display of numerical relationships, chosen so a reader can compare values more quickly than in a table alone.
graph.example: The line graph made the weekend temperature drop obvious at a glance.
graph.basic: The line diagram made the weekend temperature drop obvious.

gravity.simple: The force that pulls objects toward Earth, or the seriousness of a situation.
gravity.detailed: The attractive force between masses that gives weight; in formal writing, also the weightiness of a problem or tone.
gravity.example: The experiment showed gravity pulling the marble down the ramp at a steady increase in speed.
gravity.basic: The experiment showed the pulling force speeding the marble down the ramp.

grid.simple: A network of crossing lines, or a system of connected power or streets.
grid.detailed: A framework of squares used for maps and graphs, and also the linked network that delivers electricity or organises a city.
grid.example: The map grid helped the group give a six-figure reference for the nest.
grid.basic: The map squares helped the group give a six-figure reference for the nest.

guideline.simple: A recommended rule that helps people decide what to do.
guideline.detailed: Official or classroom advice that steers practice without always having the force of a hard law.
guideline.example: The safety guideline said no one entered the rock platform until the tide was checked.
guideline.basic: The safety advice said no one entered the rock platform until the tide was checked.

hardship.simple: A time of serious difficulty, especially from poverty, weather, or loss.
hardship.detailed: Sustained suffering or want that tests a family or community, often recorded in HASS sources after depression, drought, or war.
hardship.example: Letters from the 1930s described hardship when the wheat price collapsed.
hardship.basic: Letters from the 1930s described how hard life was when the wheat price collapsed.

harmony.simple: A pleasing agreement of sounds, colours, or people living together well.
harmony.detailed: The fitting-together of parts so none fights the others, used for music, design, and peaceful social relations.
harmony.example: The last paragraph restored harmony after the two sisters finally told the truth.
harmony.basic: The last paragraph restored peace after the two sisters finally told the truth.

hazard.simple: Something that can cause harm if people are not careful.
hazard.detailed: A source of danger in an environment or method, which risk assessments try to name, reduce, or control.
hazard.example: Wet rocks were listed as a hazard on the fieldwork permission note.
hazard.basic: Wet rocks were listed as a danger on the fieldwork permission note.

headline.simple: The large title of a news story, written to catch attention.
headline.detailed: A compact line that frames an article's angle; media study asks whether it is fair or sensational.
headline.example: The misleading headline blamed 'kids' for the litter, though the photo showed a worksite skip.
headline.basic: The misleading title blamed 'kids' for the litter, though the photo showed a worksite skip.

hierarchy.simple: A ranking in which some people or things sit above others.
hierarchy.detailed: An ordered structure of status or importance, from schools and governments to animal groups and ideas.
hierarchy.example: The novel's school hierarchy made the scholarship girl eat last for a whole term.
hierarchy.basic: The novel's school ranking made the scholarship girl eat last for a whole term.

historian.simple: A person who studies and writes about the past using evidence.
historian.detailed: A trained researcher who tests sources, compares interpretations, and explains change over time rather than repeating legend.
historian.example: A local historian showed the class original rate books from the 1890s flood.
historian.basic: A local history expert showed the class original rate books from the 1890s flood.

horizon.simple: The line where the land or sea seems to meet the sky.
horizon.detailed: The visible edge of the world in a scene, and figuratively the range of a person's future hopes or knowledge.
horizon.example: A thin plume on the horizon told the lookout the ship was still hours away.
horizon.basic: A thin plume where the sea met the sky told the lookout the ship was still hours away.

hostility.simple: Strong unfriendly feeling or behaviour toward a person or group.
hostility.detailed: Open enmity that may appear as insults, exclusion, or violence, and which HASS texts often trace to fear or competing claims.
hostility.example: Growing hostility between the two towns began after the shared well ran dry.
hostility.basic: Growing unfriendly feeling between the two towns began after the well ran dry.

household.simple: The people who live together in one home, and the home they share.
household.detailed: A domestic unit used in HASS and statistics to count families, spending, and daily routines under one roof.
household.example: Each household on the street was asked to weigh its soft-plastic recycling for a week.
household.basic: Each home on the street was asked to weigh its soft-plastic recycling for a week.

humanity.simple: All people, or the kindness we show because others are human too.
humanity.detailed: The human species as a whole, and also the compassionate quality that literature and civics praise when people refuse cruelty.
humanity.example: The letter asked readers to remember their shared humanity during the refugee debate.
humanity.basic: The letter asked readers to remember other people's dignity during the refugee debate.

acute.simple: Very sharp, sudden, or serious, rather than mild or slow.
acute.detailed: Describes an angle less than 90 degrees, or a problem or feeling that is intense and often short-lived compared with a chronic one.
acute.example: There was an acute shortage of shade cloth after three heatwave days in a row.
acute.basic: There was a sudden, serious shortage of shade cloth after three heatwave days.

adequate.simple: Enough for the purpose, though not luxurious.
adequate.detailed: Meeting the required standard in quantity or quality, used when 'good' would hide whether something actually suffices.
adequate.example: Two quotes were not adequate evidence for such a sweeping claim about the whole suburb.
adequate.basic: Two quotes were not enough evidence for such a sweeping claim.

adjacent.simple: Next to something, sharing a side or border.
adjacent.detailed: Lying beside another object, room, or region so the two touch or immediately neighbour each other.
adjacent.example: The adjacent wetland flooded first, then the oval at the bottom of the slope.
adjacent.basic: The wetland next door flooded first, then the oval.

adverse.simple: Harmful or unfavourable, working against what you want.
adverse.detailed: Describes conditions, effects, or publicity that make a result worse, common in science and weather writing.
adverse.example: Adverse weather cancelled the rock-platform lesson, so the class used photographs instead.
adverse.basic: Bad weather cancelled the rock-platform lesson, so the class used photographs.

aesthetic.simple: Concerned with beauty and how something looks or feels as art.
aesthetic.detailed: Relating to artistic taste and sensory pleasure, used when a writer judges design, not only usefulness.
aesthetic.example: The architect's aesthetic choice of pale timber made the library feel calmer than the old hall.
aesthetic.basic: The architect's look-and-feel choice of pale timber made the library feel calmer.

aggressive.simple: Ready to attack, or pushing very hard to get a result.
aggressive.detailed: Showing hostility or an overly forceful style, in people, animals, or tactics that leave little room for others.
aggressive.example: An aggressive tone in the opening paragraph made the marker doubt the writer's fairness.
aggressive.basic: An attacking tone in the opening paragraph made the marker doubt the writer's fairness.

ambitious.detailed: Showing a strong desire for success or a plan that aims high, with both courage and the risk of overreaching.
ambitious.example: The ambitious plan to map every drain in the suburb needed three more volunteers.
ambitious.basic: The demanding plan to map every drain in the suburb needed three more volunteers.

analogous.simple: Similar in a useful way, even if the two things are not the same.
analogous.detailed: Comparable in function or pattern, so one case can help explain another without claiming they are identical.
analogous.example: The teacher said a battery is analogous to a water tank, but only for thinking about stored energy.
analogous.basic: The teacher said a battery is like a water tank, but only for thinking about stored energy.

anonymous.simple: With the name unknown or deliberately hidden.
anonymous.detailed: Unidentified, so a writer, donor, or source cannot be named; useful for safety, but weaker if accountability is needed.
anonymous.example: An anonymous letter warned the paper about the leaking chemical drums.
anonymous.basic: A letter with no name warned the paper about the leaking chemical drums.

anxious.simple: Worried or uneasy about what might happen.
anxious.detailed: Feeling nervous tension before a test, meeting, or threat; in literature it colours a character's inner voice.
anxious.example: He felt anxious before the scholarship paper, so he practised one timed section each night.
anxious.basic: He felt worried before the scholarship paper, so he practised one timed section each night.

applicable.simple: Relevant and able to be used in this case.
applicable.detailed: Fit to be applied: a rule, method, or example that actually covers the situation in front of you.
applicable.example: The bushfire rule was applicable to camp stoves, not only to open fires in the national park.
applicable.basic: The bushfire rule covered camp stoves, not only open fires in the park.

apprehensive.simple: Nervous because you expect something difficult.
apprehensive.detailed: Uneasy in advance of a possible harm or failure, more thoughtful than simple fear and often shown in careful hesitation.
apprehensive.example: She felt apprehensive about reading her poem aloud, yet she still stood up.
apprehensive.basic: She felt nervous about reading her poem aloud, yet she still stood up.

arbitrary.simple: Based on personal choice or chance, not on a fair rule.
arbitrary.detailed: Decided without a consistent reason, so the result can look random or unjust to those who must follow it.
arbitrary.example: Choosing house captains by hair colour felt arbitrary and weakened trust in the vote.
arbitrary.basic: Choosing house captains by hair colour felt random and weakened trust in the vote.

arid.simple: Very dry, with too little rain for most crops or forests.
arid.detailed: Describes a climate or landscape of low rainfall and high evaporation, typical of inland Australian regions in science and HASS.
arid.example: The arid inland station recorded less than two hundred millimetres of rain that year.
arid.basic: The very dry inland station recorded less than two hundred millimetres of rain.

artificial.simple: Made by people rather than occurring naturally.
artificial.detailed: Produced by human design—materials, light, or even a manner—that imitates or replaces what is natural.
artificial.example: Artificial light from the oval changed which moths the class trapped after dusk.
artificial.basic: Man-made light from the oval changed which moths the class trapped after dusk.

artistic.simple: Skilled in art, or showing creative imagination.
artistic.detailed: Relating to the making or judging of art, and describing a style that values craft, colour, and original design.
artistic.example: An artistic choice of broken type made the poster look urgent without shouting.
artistic.basic: A creative choice of broken type made the poster look urgent without shouting.

assertive.simple: Stating your view firmly and clearly, without being rude.
assertive.detailed: Confidently putting a claim or need forward, a valued argument skill that differs from aggression because it still leaves space for others.
assertive.example: An assertive opening stated the claim in one sentence before the evidence began.
assertive.basic: A firm opening stated the claim in one sentence before the evidence began.

authentic.simple: Genuine and real, not copied or pretended.
authentic.detailed: True to origin or character: a source, artefact, or voice that has not been faked or emptied of its real context.
authentic.example: The museum labelled which tools were authentic artefacts and which were modern replicas.
authentic.basic: The museum labelled which tools were genuine artefacts and which were modern replicas.

automatic.simple: Working by itself, without a person doing each step.
automatic.detailed: Self-operating through a mechanism or habit, so action continues once the system is set, sometimes without careful thought.
automatic.example: The automatic watering system still ran during the storm, which wasted stored tank water.
automatic.basic: The self-running watering system still ran during the storm, which wasted tank water.

autonomous.simple: Able to govern or decide for yourself, without outside control.
autonomous.detailed: Self-ruling, used for people, robots, or regions that set their own course within agreed limits.
autonomous.example: The island community stayed autonomous in local planning even after joining the larger council.
autonomous.basic: The island community stayed self-governing in local planning even after joining the larger council.

awkward.simple: Clumsy in movement, or uncomfortable in a social moment.
awkward.detailed: Lacking ease: a body that knocks things, a silence that feels wrong, or a sentence that will not sit smoothly.
awkward.example: An awkward silence followed when nobody wanted to admit who had left the gate open.
awkward.basic: An uncomfortable silence followed when nobody wanted to admit who had left the gate open.

barren.simple: Too poor to grow plants, or empty of useful results.
barren.detailed: Infertile land or a lifeless stretch; figuratively, a search or year that yields nothing of value.
barren.example: The barren hillside grew only saltbush after years of overgrazing.
barren.basic: The bare hillside grew only saltbush after years of overgrazing.

biased.simple: Unfairly leaning toward one side instead of judging on evidence.
biased.detailed: Showing prejudice in selection, wording, or sampling so a conclusion is tilted before the facts are fully weighed.
biased.example: A biased sample of only the sports teams could not represent the whole school's view.
biased.basic: A one-sided sample of only the sports teams could not represent the whole school.

bleak.simple: Bare, cold, or without much hope.
bleak.detailed: Describes a setting or outlook that feels exposed and joyless, used in literary description of weather, places, or futures.
bleak.example: A bleak wind off the bay made the wooden jetty sound like it might split.
bleak.basic: A cold, joyless wind off the bay made the wooden jetty sound like it might split.

blunt.simple: Saying something too directly, or having an edge that is not sharp.
blunt.detailed: In literary and argument settings, speech that is plain to the point of roughness; physically, a tool that no longer cuts cleanly.
blunt.example: His blunt comment—'that paragraph does nothing'—was true, but it stung.
blunt.basic: His too-direct comment—'that paragraph does nothing'—was true, but it stung.

bold.simple: Brave and willing to take a risk, or strong and easy to notice.
bold.detailed: Showing courage in action or a striking style in design and writing that refuses to stay timid or faint.
bold.example: A bold claim in the first line is fine if the next paragraph can prove it.
bold.basic: A daring claim in the first line is fine if the next paragraph can prove it.

bound.simple: Certain to happen, or tied by a duty or limit.
bound.detailed: Obliged by a rule, promise, or destination, and also statistically or logically sure unless something unusual intervenes.
bound.example: The team was bound by the rules to replay the last point after the whistle error.
bound.basic: The team had to replay the last point after the whistle error.

brittle.simple: Hard but easy to snap, with little bend.
brittle.detailed: Describes materials that fracture instead of flexing, and figuratively a mood or peace that can shatter under slight pressure.
brittle.example: The brittle plastic snapped when the sample tray was left in the sun.
brittle.basic: The easily snapped plastic broke when the sample tray was left in the sun.

broad.simple: Wide in space, or covering many kinds of things.
broad.detailed: Having large width, or a range of meaning that includes several cases; academic writing sometimes needs a narrower word instead.
broad.example: A broad definition of 'rubbish' hid the difference between food scraps and soft plastic.
broad.basic: A wide definition of 'rubbish' hid the difference between food scraps and soft plastic.

brutal.simple: Cruel and violent, showing little care for suffering.
brutal.detailed: Savagely harsh in action or condition, used in HASS and narrative when force or weather is pitiless.
brutal.example: The source described brutal conditions on the early pastoral stations in summer.
brutal.basic: The source described cruel, harsh conditions on the early pastoral stations in summer.

chronic.simple: Lasting for a long time, especially of a problem or illness.
chronic.detailed: Persisting or frequently returning, in contrast with an acute event that is sudden and short.
chronic.example: A chronic shortage of shade trees made the western playground almost unused by November.
chronic.basic: A long-term shortage of shade trees made the western playground almost unused by November.

civic.simple: Relating to a town or city and to the duties of its citizens.
civic.detailed: Connected with public life—voting, volunteering, local government—rather than purely private or commercial concerns.
civic.example: Painting the station mural was framed as civic pride, not only as art class fun.
civic.basic: Painting the station mural was framed as town pride, not only as art class fun.

civil.simple: Polite, or relating to ordinary citizens rather than the army.
civil.detailed: Courteous in manner, and also describing non-military society, rights, and courts in HASS writing.
civil.example: A civil reply to the angry email earned more respect than a matching insult.
civil.basic: A polite reply to the angry email earned more respect than a matching insult.

classic.simple: Of lasting high quality, or typical of its kind.
classic.detailed: Judged as a standard example over time, whether a novel, design, or mistake that keeps reappearing.
classic.example: The camp narrative used a classic journey structure: leave, test, return changed.
classic.basic: The camp narrative used a typical journey structure: leave, test, return changed.

clinical.simple: Relating to medical treatment of patients, or coolly factual.
clinical.detailed: Based on work with real patients rather than only theory; in tone, detached and precise, sometimes lacking warmth.
clinical.example: The nurse's clinical notes recorded pulse and temperature without extra story.
clinical.basic: The nurse's medical notes recorded pulse and temperature without extra story.

cognitive.simple: Relating to thinking, knowing, and remembering.
cognitive.detailed: Concerned with mental processes such as attention, memory, and reasoning, used in science and education writing.
cognitive.example: Too many fonts on one slide increased cognitive load and hid the actual result.
cognitive.basic: Too many fonts on one slide made thinking harder and hid the actual result.

collective.simple: Done or shared by a group rather than one person.
collective.detailed: Belonging to people acting together, so responsibility, ownership, or voice is joint.
collective.example: Cleaning the creek was a collective effort, not a job dumped on one class.
collective.basic: Cleaning the creek was a shared effort, not a job dumped on one class.

colonial.simple: Relating to a colony or to the period when one country ruled another.
colonial.detailed: Connected with a ruling power's settlements overseas, and with the settler-era structures that still shape Australian HASS debates.
colonial.example: The unit compared colonial land maps with later native-title decisions.
colonial.basic: The unit compared settler-era land maps with later native-title decisions.

commercial.simple: Related to buying, selling, and making a profit.
commercial.detailed: Designed for trade rather than purely public, artistic, or domestic purposes; also used for advertising tone.
commercial.example: Commercial use of the hall was banned on weeknights so homework clubs could stay free.
commercial.basic: Business use of the hall was banned on weeknights so homework clubs could stay free.

commonplace.simple: Ordinary and familiar, not surprising any more.
commonplace.detailed: So usual that it no longer attracts notice; academic writing may challenge a familiar idea that people have stopped testing.
commonplace.example: Plastic snack wrappers had become so commonplace that nobody counted them as litter at first.
commonplace.basic: Plastic snack wrappers had become so ordinary that nobody counted them as litter at first.

compact.simple: Closely packed, or small but complete.
compact.detailed: Occupying little space because parts are efficiently arranged; science may also use it for dense materials.
compact.example: A compact design let the weather station fit on one fence post without shading the gauge.
compact.basic: A small, tightly packed design let the weather station fit on one fence post.

compassionate.simple: Feeling and showing kindness toward people who are suffering.
compassionate.detailed: Responding to others' pain with care and a wish to help, a valued quality in characters and in civic decisions.
compassionate.example: A compassionate response to the flood families was more than a photo; it was dry beds and meals.
compassionate.basic: A kind response to the flood families was more than a photo; it was dry beds and meals.

compatible.simple: Able to exist or work together without conflict.
compatible.detailed: Fitting another system, person, or idea so parts function jointly; science and design use it for devices and materials too.
compatible.example: The new sensor was not compatible with the old laptop, so the data never saved.
compatible.basic: The new sensor did not work with the old laptop, so the data never saved.

compelling.simple: So strong or interesting that it is hard to ignore.
compelling.detailed: Holding attention or forcing agreement because the evidence, story, or need is powerful.
compelling.zh: 有说服力的；引人入胜的
compelling.example: The photographs were compelling evidence that the drain still dumped silt into the lagoon.
compelling.basic: The photographs were strong evidence that the drain still dumped silt into the lagoon.

competent.simple: Having the skill to do a task well enough.
competent.detailed: Adequately able: trained and reliable, even if not brilliant, so others can trust the work.
competent.example: A competent lab partner checked the units before anyone poured the solution.
competent.basic: A capable lab partner checked the units before anyone poured the solution.

competitive.simple: Eager to win, or involving rivalry between people or groups.
competitive.detailed: Marked by contest for places, marks, or markets; can drive effort or crowd out cooperation.
competitive.example: Entry to the scholarship school was competitive, so the writing had to be precise, not fluffy.
competitive.basic: Entry to the scholarship school involved rivalry, so the writing had to be precise.

complementary.simple: Combining well so each part supplies what the other lacks.
complementary.detailed: Completing one another (not 'free' or flattering); colours, skills, or sources that together make a fuller whole.
complementary.example: The two reports were complementary: one had numbers, the other had interviews.
complementary.basic: The two reports fitted together: one had numbers, the other had interviews.

complete.simple: Having all the needed parts, or finished.
complete.detailed: Whole and lacking nothing required, or brought to an end so no further essential work remains.
complete.example: A complete answer named the cause, the evidence, and the remaining doubt.
complete.basic: A finished answer named the cause, the evidence, and the remaining doubt.

complicated.simple: Made of many parts and therefore hard to understand or do.
complicated.detailed: Intricate rather than simple, with connections that a careful writer must unpack instead of calling the topic 'messy'.
complicated.example: The recycling rule looked complicated until they sorted it into three clear bins.
complicated.basic: The recycling rule looked hard and tangled until they sorted it into three clear bins.

composed.simple: Calm and in control of your feelings.
composed.detailed: Self-possessed under pressure, a literary quality of characters who do not scatter when a scene turns hard.
composed.example: She stayed composed at the lectern even when the microphone squealed.
composed.basic: She stayed calm at the lectern even when the microphone squealed.

compulsory.simple: Required by a rule; you do not have a free choice.
compulsory.detailed: Obligatory under school, civic, or legal authority, contrasted with optional activities people may decline.
compulsory.example: In Australia, voting in federal elections is compulsory for enrolled adults.
compulsory.basic: In Australia, voting in federal elections is required for enrolled adults.

conceited.simple: Too proud of yourself and your own importance.
conceited.detailed: Vain in a way that bores or hurts others, a character flaw that narratives often punish or gently mock.
conceited.example: A conceited remark about 'ordinary readers' made the scholarship panel wince.
conceited.basic: A vain remark about 'ordinary readers' made the scholarship panel wince.

concise.simple: Short and clear, with no wasted words.
concise.detailed: Packed with meaning in a small space, a prized academic quality when every sentence still stays exact.
concise.example: A concise summary of the creek data fitted on one slide without dropping the units.
concise.basic: A short, clear summary of the creek data fitted on one slide without dropping the units.
